newsitem.title: USA: Europe not intending grain price war - EU official.
newsitem.headline: Europe not intending grain price war - EU official.

text.p: Europe has neither the money nor the desire to provoke an international grain price war through the use of export subsidies, a senior EU official said in remarks to be delivered at the U.S. Department of Agriculture's annual Agricultural Outlook Conference.

"Although export refunds have been re-introduced to enable Community exporters to follow the downward movement of world prices, we have neither the budgetary resources nor the intention of provoking a price war," said D.F. Roberts, deputy director general of the European Commission in a speech to be delivered Tuesday.

Roberts said that given Europe's big cereals production last year -- which he estimated at over 200 million tonnes -- and the current competitive export environment, it will be difficult to increase Europe's export volume and said a "significant" rebuilding of intervention stocks by the end of the season "seems inevitable."

Roberts said European officials are debating the direction that EU agricultural policy should take for the next decade, and noted that there are two predominant schools of thought in Europe -- one which argues for a liberalized policy with less support and the end of production restrictions, and the more traditional view of maintaining current farm structures with prices supports, output controls and import protection.
The official maintained that even large price cuts across the board would not lead to major reductions in European agricultural production, but would only change the structure of EU agriculture.
"They (price cuts) would not drive us off world markets," said Roberts.

Roberts said that production control measures have a greater impact on output than price policy, but that such measures can work only with "an adequate level" of import protection, and added that they are difficult to defend unless other major players also have such restrictions in place.
Roberts concluded that in an open trading environment, European farmers have not choice but to compete on the world markets.
